desc:
A hiker walks from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell of a rectangular grid, moving one step right or one step down at a time. A cell with value 1 contains a wall and a cell with value 0 is open. The hiker has a pickaxe that lets them pass through at most one wall cell during the whole walk (the start and destination cells count too if they are walls).

Return the number of different routes that use at most one wall cell, modulo 1,000,000,007.

grid = [[0,1],
        [1,0]]   ->  2   (each of the two routes crosses exactly one wall)
grid = [[0,1,0],
        [1,1,0],
        [0,0,0]] ->  2
hints: Counting routes that avoid all walls is the easy part. The new twist is a resource (one pickaxe use) that a route may or may not have spent.
Store two numbers per cell: routes that arrive having used the pickaxe 0 times and routes that arrive having used it exactly once.

Entering an open cell keeps both counts. Entering a wall cell moves every unused-pickaxe route into the used column, and routes that already spent it are dropped. The answer is the sum of both counts at the destination.
editorial: Let a[r][c] be the number of routes into (r, c) using no wall so far and b[r][c] those using exactly one. First gather what comes from the cell above and the cell to the left: a' = a[r-1][c] + a[r][c-1], b' = b[r-1][c] + b[r][c-1] (for the start cell, a' = 1, b' = 0).

If the cell is open the new values are a = a', b = b'. If it is a wall, every route that has not used the pickaxe now uses it: a = 0, b = a', and routes in b' would need a second wall so they vanish. The answer is a + b at the bottom-right cell. A single array of pairs per row gives O(n) memory and O(m · n) time. The same layering trick (an extra dimension for a small budget) works for any 'at most j walls' variant at O(m · n · j).
